Reading a Comodulogram

Reviving CFC · a walkthrough with working parts

Reading a Comodulogram

What your MATLAB actually does to a raw trace, one step at a time — with sliders, so you can break each step and watch what happens.

The whole thing in four sentences

Take one channel of brain signal. Pull out a slow rhythm and a fast rhythm. Ask: when the slow rhythm is at a particular point in its cycle, is the fast rhythm reliably louder? A comodulogram runs that question for ~1 900 pairs of slow and fast frequencies and paints the answers as a map.

That's it. Everything below is unpacking those four sentences, plus the five ways the map can fool you.

Every graph on this page is built from made-up data where I set the true answer by hand. That's the point: if you know what went in, you can tell whether the method reports it correctly. Nothing here reads a real recording.

Part 1

What we are looking for

A hippocampal recording is a jumble of oscillations at once. Two of them matter here:

  • a slow one — theta, say 8 cycles per second. Big, obvious, easy to see by eye.
  • a fast one — gamma, say 80 cycles per second. Small, and it sits on top of the slow one like ripples on a swell.

Phase–amplitude couplingThe full name of what this pipeline measures. "Phase" = where you are in the slow cycle. "Amplitude" = how loud the fast rhythm is. Coupling = the two are related. is the claim that the fast ripples are not equally loud everywhere along the slow swell — they bunch up at one part of the cycle.

Drag the slider below. At 0 the fast rhythm is the same size everywhere. Turn it up and it starts clumping.

Slow swell, fast ripplesdrag the slider

Grey line: the raw signal, everything mixed together — this is all you ever get from the electrode. Blue: the slow rhythm alone. Orange: how loud the fast rhythm is, moment to moment. Coupling is when the orange line rises and falls in step with the blue one.

At high noise you can still see it in the orange line but not in the grey one. That's the whole reason this pipeline exists: the effect is real and invisible to the eye, so you need arithmetic to pull it out.

Part 2 · Step one of the code

Splitting slow from fast

To ask about two rhythms separately, you first have to separate them. That's what a filter does.

Filter, in plain terms

A bandpass filter"Band" = a range of frequencies. "Pass" = let it through. So: let through only the wiggles between two speeds, silence everything else. is a sieve for wiggle speed. You give it two numbers — a low cutoff and a high cutoff — and it hands back a copy of your signal containing only the wiggles between those speeds. Everything slower and everything faster is removed.

Try it. The top trace is a raw signal. Move the two cutoffs and watch what survives.

A filter is a sieve for wiggle speedmove both cutoffs

Set it to 6–10 and you get the slow swell. Set it to 65–95 and you get the fast ripples, with the slow swell gone. Set it wide and you get the mess back. The pipeline does exactly this, 88 times, with 88 different cutoff pairs.

Why filtfilt runs the filter twice

Here's the bit you asked about. Filtering is not free — a filter has to look at the signal to decide what to keep, and looking takes time. Concretely, a filter's output at a given moment is a weighted mix of the samples just before it. That mix inevitably comes out slightly late.

The analogy

Imagine smoothing a bumpy road by averaging the last ten metres of height. Your smoothed road is a fine smooth road — but it is shifted forward, because at every point you're reporting where the road was, not where it is. Every hill appears a bit further along than it really is.

For this analysis a shift is fatal. The entire measurement is "was the fast rhythm loud at this point of the slow cycle" — if the filter moved the slow cycle ten milliseconds to the right, every answer is wrong by ten milliseconds.

The fix is embarrassingly simple. Run the filter forwards; the output is shifted late. Then reverse the signal and run the same filter again; that second pass shifts it late in the reversed direction, which is early in the original direction. The two shifts are equal and opposite, so they cancel exactly. Flip it back and you have a filtered signal with zero timing error. That is filtfilt — "filter, then filter the flipped copy".

Click through the three states below and watch the peak marker.

One pass shifts it. Two passes don't.click the buttons
Timing error  —

Grey: the true slow rhythm hidden in the signal. Blue: what the filter returns. Dashed verticals mark the true peaks. Sharper filters shift more — turn sharpness up on one pass and watch the error grow, then switch to two passes and watch it go to zero regardless.

In the lab code this is the line filtfilt(filtwts, 1, data) inside eegfilt.m. It is why nobody has to correct for filter delay anywhere else in the pipeline.

Part 3 · Step two of the code

Two words: phase and envelope

After filtering you have two clean signals: a slow one and a fast one. The code now throws away most of each, keeping exactly one number per sample from each.

From the slow signal it keeps the phase

Phase is just "where are we in the cycle right now", written as an angle. Think of a clock hand going round once per cycle: pointing right is the start, straight up is a quarter of the way, pointing left is halfway, and so on. Because it's an angle it's usually written in radiansA way of measuring angles where a full turn is 2π ≈ 6.28 instead of 360. Half a turn is π ≈ 3.14. The code uses radians because that's what MATLAB's angle() returns., running from −π to +π, which is the same as −180° to +180°.

Phase says nothing about how big the slow wave is. A huge theta cycle and a tiny one both go through the same phases.

From the fast signal it keeps the envelope

The envelope — also called the amplitude — is the outline traced around the fast wiggles. If you drew a smooth curve touching the top of every fast peak, that's the envelope. It says how loud the fast rhythm is at each moment and ignores where in its own cycle it happens to be.

What the Hilbert transform is for

Getting "the angle right now" and "the loudness right now" out of a wiggly line isn't obvious — a plain sine wave passes through zero twice per cycle, and at those moments you can't read off either quantity from the value alone. The Hilbert transformA standard signal-processing operation that produces a second copy of your signal shifted a quarter cycle. Pairing the original with the shifted copy gives you a rotating vector instead of a single number. solves this by manufacturing a second copy of the signal shifted a quarter of a cycle. Plot the original against the shifted copy and instead of a line going up and down you get a vector going round in a circle. Its angle is the phase. Its length is the envelope. Both, at every sample, unambiguously.

That's the whole content of angle(hilbert(x)) and abs(hilbert(x)) in the MATLAB.

Scrub through time below and watch the three views stay in lockstep.

Phase is a clock hand. Envelope is an outline.drag through time
Phase  — Bin (of 18)  — Fast-rhythm loudness  —

Left: the slow rhythm with a marker at the current moment, and the fast rhythm's envelope above it. Right: the same moment as a clock hand, sitting in one of 18 wedges. Every sample of the recording gets sorted into one of those 18 wedges, and its fast-rhythm loudness is dropped into that wedge's bucket.

Part 4 · Step three of the code

Eighteen buckets, then one number

Now the actual measurement, which is simpler than it sounds:

  1. Cut the slow cycle into 18 wedges of 20° each.
  2. For every sample in the recording, note which wedge its slow-phase falls in, and drop its fast-envelope value into that wedge's bucket.
  3. Average each bucket. You now have 18 numbers: the typical fast-rhythm loudness at each part of the slow cycle.
  4. Ask one question of those 18 numbers: how far from flat are they?

Flat means no coupling — the fast rhythm was equally loud everywhere in the slow cycle. Lumpy means coupling.

Turning "how lumpy" into a number

First the 18 averages are rescaled to add up to 1, which turns them into proportions — "what share of the total loudness sat in this wedge". Call those P₁…P₁₈. Then the code measures their lumpiness with entropyA measure of how spread-out a set of proportions is. Maximum when everything is equal, lower when the mass piles up in a few places. Comes from information theory; here it's just being used as a flatness meter.:

flattest possible log 18 = 2.890 what we observed H = − Σ Pj log Pj the shortfall log 18 − H bigger = lumpier = more coupling as a fraction MI = (log 18 − H) / log 18

Entropy is largest when the 18 proportions are all equal, and drops as they pile up unevenly. So MI is the missing entropy, expressed as a fraction of the most that could be missing. Zero means perfectly flat. One would mean every bit of fast-rhythm loudness happened inside a single 20° wedge, which never happens — so real values sit in the third decimal place.

Mathematically this is the Kullback–Leibler divergenceA standard measure of how different one distribution is from another. Here: how different the observed 18 proportions are from a perfectly flat set of 18 proportions. Dividing it by log 18 just rescales it to run from 0 to 1. of P from flat, divided by log 18. That's all "normalised entropy index" in the Tort papers means.

Play with it. The bars are the 18 buckets; the number is MI.

The 18 buckets, and the number they collapse tothree sliders
MI  — entropy H  — shortfall  — vs flat (log 18)  2.8904

Set coupling to 0 and notice MI does not reach zero — it lands somewhere around 0.002. Then pull recording length down and watch that floor climb. With finite data the 18 buckets are never exactly equal, so MI is always a bit positive. This matters, and it comes back as trap 4.

Part 5 · Step four of the code

One number becomes a map

Everything so far gives one MI, for one pair of bands — say "8 Hz phase, 80 Hz amplitude". But you don't know in advance which pair matters. So the code sweeps a grid: every slow band on one axis, every fast band on the other, one MI per crossing point. That grid, drawn as a colour map, is the comodulogram.

Reading the axes

Left–right (x) = the slow frequency, the one whose phase is doing the organising.
Up–down (y) = the fast frequency, the one whose loudness is being organised.
Colour = MI at that crossing point.
A bright spot at x = 8, y = 80 reads: "the loudness of the 80 Hz rhythm is organised by the phase of the 8 Hz rhythm."

The map below is computed live in your browser from a signal you control. Click any cell to see the 18 buckets behind it.

Live comodulogramclick a cell to open it up
brightest cell  — its MI  —

The colour scale rescales to the map's own maximum, exactly as the MATLAB does — so always read the colour bar, not the brightness. The "fast-filter width" slider at 0 means "match what eegfilt actually delivers"; any other value fixes the width in Hz, as the drivers claim to.

Three experiments worth two minutes.
1 · Push fast-filter width to 10 Hz — what the code says it uses — and watch the blob disappear even though the coupling is still there. That's trap 2.
2 · Set coupling strength to 0 and spikes to 2/s. A map appears with no coupling in the signal at all. That's trap 3.
3 · Pull recording length down with coupling at 0. The whole map brightens. That's trap 4.

Each figure is several plots side by side or stacked. The bold a, b, c… in the top-left corner of each plot are just labels, so the caption can say "in b" instead of "in the middle one". Part 7

Five ways the map lies

None of these are mistakes in your lab's code. They are properties of the method as published, and they show up clearly in simulation because there the true answer is known. They matter most when you are comparing groups — which is exactly what the PTEN work does.

TRAP 1

The filters are much wider than the code claims

eegfilt.m doesn't let you choose how sharp the filter is. It works it out for you:

filtorder = 3 · fix(srate / locutoff)

In words: make the filter about three cycles of the lower cutoff long. A filter's sharpness depends on how many cycles it spans, so "always three cycles" means "always the same relative sharpness" — roughly a third of the centre frequency, whatever passband you asked for.

What that costs you

You ask for a 10 Hz-wide window at 200 Hz. You get a 60 Hz-wide one. You ask for a 0.5 Hz-wide window at 26 Hz. You get a 7.8 Hz-wide one — while the grid places its next column only 0.5 Hz away, so neighbouring columns there are near-copies of each other.

Band as written in the driverfilter lengthWhat the filter actually passesWidth askedWidth got
1 : 1.5 Hz  (phase)9 767 taps1.05 – 1.46 Hz0.50.42 Hz
8 : 8.5 Hz  (phase)1 219 taps7.17 – 9.59 Hz0.52.42 Hz
26 : 26.5 Hz  (phase)377 taps22.77 – 30.54 Hz0.57.77 Hz
20 : 30 Hz  (amp)487 taps20.90 – 29.43 Hz108.54 Hz
80 : 90 Hz  (amp)121 taps73.65 – 98.62 Hz1024.97 Hz
200 : 210 Hz  (amp)49 taps178.05 – 238.08 Hz1060.03 Hz

Measured at 3 255 Hz, which is what read_csc(file, 10) gives you from a 32 556 Hz Neuralynx file. TapsThe number of samples a filter looks at to produce one output sample. More taps = sharper filter, but also more of the signal smeared into each output point. shrink as the frequency rises, which is why the high rows are so broad.

TRAP 2

Half the map physically cannot show coupling

This one follows from trap 1 and it is the most consequential.

When a slow rhythm at fp makes a fast rhythm at fa get louder and quieter, the resulting signal is not pure fa any more. Modulating something always creates two extra tones on either side, at fa − fp and fa + fp. Those two extras are the modulation: if your amplitude filter is too narrow to include them, it removes them, the envelope comes out flat, and MI reports nothing.

So the filter has to be at least 2 × fp wide. Combine with trap 1 (real width ≈ 0.30 × fa) and you get a hard ceiling:

highest detectable slow frequency ≈ 0.15 × fast frequency

Below that line the coupling shows up. Above it, identical coupling reads as zero. In Figure 7 the simulated coupling is turned up to maximum at every point of the grid and nothing else varies — MI still ranges from 0.072 down to 0.00001.

What this means for your maps

A 4 Hz effect is visible almost anywhere. An 8 Hz effect is badly attenuated below about 55 Hz. A 20 Hz effect is invisible below about 130 Hz. So the empty top-left triangle in your comodulograms is the analysis, not the tissue — and two blobs at different heights on the map are not measured on the same footing. Only compare blobs at similar fast frequencies.

Feel it: in the live map above, set fast-filter width to 10 Hz and slide the slow frequency up from 3 to 18 Hz.

TRAP 3

Sharp spikes manufacture coupling out of nothing

An interictal discharge is a very fast, very large deflection. Anything that sharp contains energy at every frequency at once — that's just what "sharp" means in frequency terms. So every amplitude band gets a simultaneous kick.

Meanwhile the same event also produces a big swing in the slow bands. So the kicks are not scattered evenly around the slow cycle; they land at a consistent phase. Loud fast activity, consistently at one phase, is precisely the pattern MI is built to detect — and it will report it, enthusiastically, from a signal containing no oscillatory coupling whatsoever.

Figure 8 is background noise plus 1.5 sharp transients per second. Nothing else. Its map peaks at MI 0.0093, twenty-one times the noise floor.

The direct problem for the PTEN comparisons

IED rate differs between genotypes, between conditions, and between layers. So any comodulogram difference you find between them is entangled with an IED-rate difference, and no statistic downstream can separate the two. Detect and mask events before running CFC, or run only on IED-free epochs, and report event rate per epoch next to the MI. The Toothy detection already in the lab's stack is the obvious source of masks.

Feel it: in the live map, coupling strength to 0, spikes to 2 per second.

TRAP 4

MI has no true zero, and longer recordings score lower

You saw this in Part 4. With a finite recording the 18 bucket averages are never exactly equal, so MI comes out positive even when there is nothing to find. The shorter the recording, the fewer samples per bucket, the more they wobble, the higher the false MI. It falls off roughly as one over the number of samples.

Measured on pure noise at one grid cell: MI = 0.0027 for a 2.5 s epoch, 0.00002 for a 320 s epoch. Two orders of magnitude from recording length alone.

The practical version

If your baseline recordings are longer than your CNO recordings, or one animal contributed shorter files, part of any group difference is just epoch length. Match durations across everything that enters the same statistic.

What a surrogate test does about it

The standard fix gives MI a scale. Take your real phase series and your real envelope, and slide one of them in time by a random amount — a surrogateA fake dataset built from your real one, with the thing you're testing deliberately destroyed. Everything else — the spectrum, the noise, the spike content — is preserved, so the surrogate tells you what MI this recording produces by chance.. Everything about both signals is preserved except their alignment, so whatever MI you get is what this particular recording produces by chance. Do it 400 times and you have a distribution of chance values. Your real MI is then reportable as "so many standard deviations above chance", which is comparable across channels, animals and epoch lengths in a way that raw MI is not.

TRAP 5

The colour scale is doing the talking

contourf(..., 30, 'lines', 'none') with no CLim stretches the colours to fit whatever range that particular map happens to have. Since the pipeline saves one figure per channel, no two of your saved figures are on the same scale unless you put them there. A map that looks dramatic may top out at MI 0.0004.

The jet colormap compounds it: its abrupt jumps from blue to cyan to yellow to red invent visual edges where the underlying surface is perfectly smooth, so smooth noise reads as structure. The 30 discrete contour levels do the same thing.

All three panels in Figure 11 are the same no-coupling recording.

Part 8

Your grid, and what the R script does to it

Specifics for this repo, so the numbers in your .mat files have addresses.

SettingValue in newFCSE.mMeaning
Slow axis1 : 0.5 : 26 Hz51 bands. Plotted at their centres, 1.25 → 26.25 Hz
Fast axis20 : 5 : 200 Hz37 bands. Plotted at their centres, 25 → 205 Hz
PTEN driver20 : 5 : 300 Hzfast axis opened to 300 Hz to look for pHFO coupling
Bucketsnbin = 1820° each. Change it and every MI changes
Line noise59–61 Hz notchthe PTEN driver widens this to 55–65 Hz
Cells per channel51 × 37 = 1 887each one an 18-bucket histogram collapsed to a single number

Because the axes are plotted at band centres but the matrix is indexed by band starts, cell (4, 4) of the transposed matrix is 2.75 Hz slow by 40 Hz fast — which is exactly what the comment in Notes_ComodAnalysis.m says, so that comment is reliable.

The four bands the R script produces

CFCReader.R reproduces Notes_ComodAnalysis.m: transpose the map so rows are fast frequencies and columns are slow frequencies, then average ranges of columns into four named bands. Converting those column numbers to Hz:

Band nameColumns averagedActual slow frequenciesWorth knowing
Delta1 : 31.25 – 2.25 Hzshares column 3 with Del-Theta
Del-Theta3 : 92.25 – 5.25 Hzshares columns 7–9 with Theta
Theta7 : 234.25 – 12.25 Hzshares column 23 with Beta
Beta23 : 4012.25 – 20.75 Hzthis is high theta / beta, not classical beta
—41 : 5121.25 – 26.25 Hzcomputed every run, never used by any band

Three consequences. The bands overlap at their shared columns, so Delta and Del-Theta are not independent measures and neither are Theta and Beta. A fifth of the slow axis is computed and thrown away. And averaging over a wide band dilutes a narrow peak — in Figure 10 the map peaks at 0.0387 while the Theta band average peaks at 0.0179, because the blob is two columns wide and the band is seventeen.

Part 9

Notes on the code as you found it

The parfor in newFCSE.m is ugly but correct

data_vector = single(length(AmpFreqVector)) creates a single number — the value 37 — not a vector of 37 slots. Then data_vector(ii,jj) = MI forces MATLAB to grow it into a mostly-empty ii × jj array. Only row ii is ever read back, and row ii does get every MI, so the output is right. It just wastes a lot of memory and will confuse the next reader. Replace with zeros(1, length(AmpFreqVector)) and data_vector(jj) = MI.

The matrix gets transposed twice on the way out

newFCSE.m saves it already transposed with three metadata columns bolted on (z = 37 repeats them once per fast-frequency row). TRANSpose_comodulograms.m transposes again, for the older drivers that save it the other way. Check the orientation of any .mat before reading it rather than assuming; the R scripts treat columns as slow frequencies.

The notch differs between drivers

59–61 Hz in newFCSE.m, 55–65 Hz in the PTEN driver. The wider one deletes a real 10 Hz slice of the fast axis. Results produced by the two are not the same analysis.

There is already a cross-check in the repo

04_reference/ft_crossfrequencyanalysis.m is FieldTrip's version, and it implements mvl (mean vector length) alongside mi. MVL keeps the preferred phase that MI throws away. Running it on a handful of channels is a cheap sanity check: a real blob should appear in both.

Things that will simply stop a run

Hardcoded absolute paths in nearly every driver; cd = path_xls assigning to the built-in cd instead of calling it; TRANSpose_comodulograms.m pulling the file number out with the fixed offset baseFileName(38:end-4), which only works for one exact filename length. None of these change the arithmetic.

Part 10

If you revive this

Roughly in order of how much each one changes the conclusions:

  1. Mask IEDs before computing anything. Otherwise trap 3 rides along with every group comparison in the dataset.
  2. Match epoch lengths across everything entering the same statistic — or z-score MI against a per-channel surrogate null. Ideally both.
  3. Fix CLim across any set of figures you plan to compare by eye, and stop using jet.
  4. Set the fast-filter width from the slow frequency instead of fixing it at 10 Hz. Something like ampBW = max(10, 2.5*fp) makes the whole grid comparable rather than just its lower-right corner.
  5. Save MeanAmp, not just MI. ModIndex_v2 already returns it. Preferred phase is free at that point and is often more interpretable, especially across CA1 layers.
  6. Thin the slow axis. 51 columns imply a resolution the filters cannot deliver. 0.5 Hz steps below ~5 Hz and wider steps above would cost nothing and mislead less.
All figures and every number on this page come from synthetic data generated by Reviving CFC/05_explainer/ — one script per figure, plus verify.py, which asserts each quoted value (21 checks, all passing). The interactive panels compute everything live in your browser. Nothing here reads a recording.
